playlist.name: Pink Floyd Essentials
playlist.description: Some bands turn into shorthand for a certain sound or style, and Pink Floyd belongs among that elite group. The very name connotes something specific: an elastic, echoing, mind-bending sound that evokes the chasms of space. Pink Floyd grounded that limitless sound with exacting explorations of mundane matters of ego, mind, memory and heart, touching upon madness, alienation, narcissism and society on their concept albums of the 1970s. Of these concept records, ‘Dark Side of the Moon’ resonated strongest, earning new audiences year after year, decade after decade, and its longevity makes sense. That 1973 album distilled the wild psychedelia of their early years — that brief, heady period when they were fronted by Syd Barrett — into a slow, sculpted, widescreen epic masterminded by Roger Waters, the bassist who was the band’s de facto leader in the ’70s. Waters fueled Pink Floyd’s golden years, conceiving such epics as ‘Wish You Were Here’ and ‘The Wall,’ but the band survived his departure in the ’80s, with guitarist David Gilmour stepping to the forefront on ‘A Momentary Lapse of Reason’ and ‘The Division Bell.’ Throughout the years, drummer Nick Mason and keyboardist Rick Wright appeared in some capacity, and the group’s sonic signature was always evident: a wide, expansive sound that was instantly recognizable as their own, yet was adopted by all manner of bands, from guitar-worshiping metalheads to freaky, hippie, ambient electronic duos. Unlike almost any of their peers, Pink Floyd played to both sides of the aisle: They were rooted in the blues, but their heart belonged to the future, a dichotomy that made them a quintessentially modern 20th-century band. (Photo and bio: Rovi)

(Cover: Pink Floyd in 1967 / Photo: Andrew Whittuck/Redferns)

playlist.name: Pink Floyd Evolution: The Gilmour Years
Pink Floyd Evolution: The Gilmour Years

(Cover: Pink Floyd in 1987 / Photo: Ross Marino/Getty Images)

playlist.name: Pink Floyd Evolution: Prog-Rock Giants
playlist.description: This playlist features the Floyd as prog auteurs, elevating the rock album to new levels of cultural importance and selling patient, surreal music about madness and the travesties of humanity in numbers great enough to bolster the entire recording industry. (Photo: Rovi)

playlist.name: Tracks & Traces: Pink Floyd
playlist.description: Pink Floyd is one of the most influential bands in rock history, with a sprawling legacy traversing eras and genres. In this playlist we unfold the story of Pink Floyd as a keystone of popular-music influence, covering the music that inspired them, then tracing their journey through generations of impact. (Photo: Rovi)

playlist.name: Remember...the 1970s

It was a time of excess and perfection, idealism and hypocrisy, high art and high commercial value. If the 1960s sparked the cultural renaissance of the later 20th century, and the 1980s were one hell of a hangover, the ‘70s were our golden age. (Cover: Sly & the Family Stone - There's a Riot Goin' On, Epic/Sony)

playlist.name: 1977! Songs of the Year
playlist.description: Two major music trends clashed into the year 1977: The pinnacle of punk rock and the rise of disco. The Ramones, The Sex Pistols, The Stranglers, Buzzcocks and The Clash all released important punk albums this year, marking the biggest year for punk since it’s arrival merely a year before and its vanishing into post-punk a year or so later. On the other side of the spectrum, the funky and groovy disco beats continued to increase in popularity in the night clubs of New York and L.A. Bee Gees’ soundtrack to the blockbuster Saturday Night Fever fully realized the transition from the underground to mainstream. Outside and in between these to extremities, there was surely plenty of room for more classic sounding pop and rock. 1977 was not only punk and disco, but also a major year for names like Fleetwood Mac, Queen, AC/DC and Kiss. This playlist takes you through the highs of a year full of them. (Cover: David Bowie - Low, Universal)

playlist.name: 1987! Songs of the Year
playlist.description: 1987 was a significant year for epic album releases, including some of the most memorable and cherished recordings of modern times: Michael Jackson’s 'Bad', U2’s 'The Joshua Tree', Guns n’ Roses’ 'Appetite for Destruction', Prince’s 'Sign 'O’ the Times' and George Michael’s 'Faith' are just some of the titles that have helped secure 1987 a place in music history. Hip-hop innovators like Eric B & Rakim, Public Enemy, LL Cool J and Boogie Down Productions marked the beginning of a musical and cultural style that would some years later rule the world. 1987 was also a great year for alternative rock, with major titles dropping from Dinosaur Jr., Sonic Youth and Hüsker Dü, while some interesting movements in the Pacific Northwest (Soundgarden, Green River, Melvins) hinted at what's to come. But nevermind the future; from Prince to Napalm Death, this is what we remember and didn’t know we missed from the year in music 1987. (Cover: Prince - Sign 'O' the Times, Sony)

playlist.name: 1979! Songs of the Year
playlist.description: The end of an era, and the beginning of a new: Following the aftermath of punk and disco, 1979 marks the rise of electro pioneers and synth-pop and the early days of hip-hop. Massive albums by The Clash (‘London Calling’), Pink Floyd (‘The Wall’) and Michael Jackson (‘Off the Wall’) saw the light of the day, as well as early albums from The Police, Prince, and The Cure. And did music videos killed the radio stars? Find deep album cuts, forgotten gems and the biggest hit singles on this playlist with songs from 1979. [This list of yearly songs follows the rule of earliest release date.] (Cover: Joy Division - Unknown Pleasure, Warner)

playlist.name: 1969! Songs of the Year
playlist.description: 1969 was the year of the moon landing, so most everything else pale in comparison. These were the days of Nixon and Arafat, Vietnam and Woodstock, city riots and Sesame Street. 1969 was also a landmark year in the history music. The Beatles released their final studio album, but we got debut albums from Led Zeppelin, Joe Cocker, The Stooges, Nick Drake, MC5 and many more. These were the glory days for Folk rock; Creedence Clearwater Revival (three albums!), Fairport Convention (three albums!), Townes van Zandt (two albums!), Flying Burrito Brothers, Crosby, Stills & Nash, Poco and Neil Young, just to mention a few. The year will forever be remembered for the tragic events at Altamont and how the hippie era reached its zenith on the fields of Yasgur’s farm. Dylan went to Isle of Wight, Elvis returned to Memphis, Johnny Cash headed to San Quentin and Lennon went to bed. Find chosen album cuts and hit singles on this playlist with songs from 1969. [This list of yearly songs follows the rule of earliest release date.] (Cover: Nick Drake - Five Leaves Left, UMG)

playlist.name: 1967! Songs of the Year
playlist.description: The fateful year of 1967 is known as “the Summer of Love,” coined for the thousands of flower children who assembled in masses, most densely around the Haight-Ashbury district of San Francisco, as part of the counterculture movement that shaped modern history and culture. United by a common belief in change, and with the influence of psychedelic drugs, for a wonderful moment in history there was actually a common faith among an idealistic generation of youths that peace and love would conquer war and hate. Scott McKenzie might carry the anthemic torch of the era, but for many the Summer of Love turned to fall way too soon. Nevertheless, the late 1960 gave us a fair share of mind-altering music that would forever change the face of popular music. Legends like Jimi Hendrix, The Velvet Underground, The Beatles, The Doors and Pink Floyd all made albums this year that not only stand as highlights in their respective careers, but as icons in the annals of modern music. (Cover: Jimi Hendrix - Axis: Bold As Love, Sony Legacy)

playlist.name: 1968! Songs of the Year
playlist.description: Most people might whistle along to Louis Armstrong’s "What a Wonderful World," but it is rather rage and violence that follows the flowery peace rallies from the 1967 Summer of Love. The war in Vietnam intensifies with the Tet Offensive, Robert Kennedy and Martin Luther King Jr. are both being assassinated, civil rights activists clash with the law enforcement on college campuses and several US cities, including Chicago, DC and Baltimore are burning in chaotic and violent riots. Tommie Smith and John Carlos bowed their heads and raised their fists in a Black Power salute during the Mexico Summer Olympics, and the Khmer Rogue forms in Cambodia. Moviegoers are enjoying ‘2001: A Space Odyssey,' ‘Rosemary’s Baby’ or ‘The Planet of the Apes,' and the musical ‘Hair’ premieres on Broadway. Amidst all the turmoil and tension, some of the most iconic albums in the history of music are being launched: The Beatles’ ‘White Album,' Jimi Hendrix’s ‘Electric Ladyland,' Van Morrison’s ‘Astral Weeks’ and The Band’s ‘Music From the Big Pink’ are some of the many albums making 1968 an outstanding year of music. Enjoy this travel back to some of the most popular and best tracks of 1968. This list of yearly songs follows the rule of earliest release date. (Cover: Jimi Hendrix - Electric Landyland, Sony)

playlist.name: David Gilmour Essentials
playlist.description: In Pink Floyd in the mid-’70s, David Gilmour earned a reputation as perhaps the most cinematic of the rock era’s guitar gods. The language of his playing was based in the blues, but his tremendous sound was spectral rather than gloating, and his solos unspooled like melodramas. In many ways, his playing reflected the strange duality of ’70s Floyd on the whole: It was both the stuff of mega-selling classic rock and morose art music. He’d joined the Floyd in 1967, to pick up the slack caused by his schoolmate Syd Barrett’s mental illness, which often manifested onstage. As a songwriter, vocalist and guitarist in collaboration with Roger Waters, he redefined the sonic and conceptual ambition of the rock LP, but the band fractured when Waters’ oversight came to define Pink Floyd’s vision. Gilmour was able to reform the group under his leadership (and sans Waters), shepherding them through an underrated final chapter. Throughout his career, sometimes as an escape from frustrations within his iconic band, Gilmour recorded as a solo artist. This playlist features highlights from those albums. (Photo: Anton Corbijn, Sony/press)

playlist.description: George Roger Waters (b. 1943) came to fame as a member of Pink Floyd. Waters experienced every kind of success with the band, and then managed a very successful solo career.
